items.title: A tree that died yesterday is 'older' than one from 1955
items.claim: Radiocarbon dating assumes atmospheric carbon-14 is roughly constant. Nuclear weapons testing in the 1950s and 60s doubled atmospheric C-14. Trees that grew then have unusually high C-14, and a sample that died yesterday now looks older than one from 1963.
items.prompt: What is the modern correction for this 'bomb spike'?

options.text: Radiocarbon dating no longer works for anything after 1945
Calibration curves use tree rings and other archives to map measured C-14 to true age — the bomb spike actually makes recent dating MORE precise
Scientists subtract a fixed amount from all measurements after 1945
All organic material dated after 1945 is considered modern and unmeasurable

items.reveal_title: Calibration turns a bug into a feature
items.reveal:
Dendrochronology (tree ring sequences) extends back over 13,000 years and gives a year-by-year record of atmospheric C-14. The 1955 to 1963 'bomb spike' nearly doubled C-14 concentrations, then decayed away as CO2 mixed into oceans.

Forensic scientists now use this spike to date tissues with about 1-year resolution: bone, hair, even individual lenses of the eye. It turned out that lens fibre cells preserve a chemical timestamp of the year they formed. Atmospheric pollution became a precision dating tool.
items.why: Constants are assumed to be constant. Real-world calibration is more subtle and often more interesting than the textbook formula.

items.title: Lithium has a stronger 'urge' to react than sodium — and reacts more gently
items.claim: Drop sodium into water: it fizzes violently, often igniting with a yellow flame. Drop lithium into water: it floats and fizzes calmly. Yet lithium's standard electrode potential (-3.04 V) is MORE negative than sodium's (-2.71 V).
items.prompt: Why doesn't lithium react more vigorously?

options.text: Lithium's high melting point (181°C) means it stays solid during reaction; the LiOH product is less soluble than NaOH and forms a coating that slows further reaction. Sodium melts in the reaction heat and exposes fresh surface
Standard electrode potentials are wrong for lithium
Lithium does not actually react with water

items.reveal:
Lithium's small ion has a very large hydration enthalpy (-519 kJ/mol vs sodium's -406), which more than compensates for its higher ionisation energy. So thermodynamically it has the highest tendency in Group 1 to lose an electron in aqueous solution.

But reactivity at the bench is rate-controlled by surface kinetics. Sodium melts at 98°C, well below the temperature reached during reaction with water — molten sodium spreads and exposes fresh metal. Lithium melts at 181°C and stays solid.

LiOH solubility is about 12 g per 100 g water; NaOH is 109 g. The lithium product crusts on the surface and slows further attack.
items.why: The reactivity series is taught as a single ladder. Real reactivity needs both thermodynamic driving force and a kinetic pathway.

items.title: Water dissolves more things than any other liquid
items.claim: Water is called 'the universal solvent'. It dissolves more substances than any other liquid — salts, sugars, gases, many organic molecules. Yet it has only three atoms and a simple structure.
items.prompt: What makes water such a versatile solvent?

options.text: Water is highly polar (large dipole), forms hydrogen bonds with H-bond donors and acceptors, and has a high dielectric constant (around 80) that weakens ionic attractions enough for ions to separate and become solvated
Water is the only liquid on Earth that occurs naturally

items.reveal:
Water's bent shape and large O-H bond polarity give a permanent dipole moment of 1.85 debye. Each water molecule can form up to 4 hydrogen bonds — two as donor, two as acceptor.

Water's dielectric constant of about 80 (vs about 2 for hexane) means it screens ionic charges strongly: a cation and anion that would attract each other electrostatically in vacuum are 80 times less attracted in water, so they separate.

Non-polar substances (oils, wax) lack matching interactions and so won't dissolve. 'Universal' is overstating things — water is just a brilliant solvent for polar and ionic species, and we mostly care about polar and ionic species.
items.why: Water is treated as a passive background. Its chemistry actively shapes whether ions stay dissolved or precipitate.
